extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners, patent practitioners, policymakers, and other patent system stakeholders (inventors, companies, academics)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for determining whether a claim is patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. §101 (the Alice two-step framework) and for assessing related examination practices and impacts across technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice two-step framework (overall)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the Supreme Court's two-step framework (Alice) to assess patent eligibility across all claim categories and judicial exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The unified USPTO guidance combines the criteria for eligibility into a single analysis. The two-step framework is applied as steps 2A and 2B after the initial §101 category inquiry. Examiners use the framework to determine whether claims are directed to judicial exceptions and whether additional claim elements supply 'significantly more' (an inventive concept).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 — §101 statutory category inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claimed invention falls into one of the four statutory categories recited in 35 U.S.C. §101 (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the initial threshold inquiry before applying the Alice two-step framework; if the claim does not fall within a §101 category it is not eligible. (See MPEP §2106.03 and USPTO unified guidance.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A — Identify whether claim is directed to a judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the claim is 'directed to' a judicial exception (abstract ideas, laws of nature, or natural phenomena).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under USPTO practice this is step 2A of the analysis; guidance documents (2019 PEG and October 2019 Update) revised procedures for identifying abstract ideas and for determining directedness under step 2A. If a claim is not directed to a judicial exception, no further Alice analysis is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B — 'Significantly more' / inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim is directed to a judicial exception, determine whether the additional elements of the claim add 'significantly more' than the judicial exception (i.e., provide an inventive concept).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This assessment evaluates whether claim elements (individually or as an ordered combination) transform the nature of the claim into patent-eligible subject matter. The USPTO guidance treats this as step 2B of the two-step framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Well-understood, routine, conventional' is a factual determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a claim element or combination of elements is 'well understood, routine, and conventional' to a skilled artisan is a factual inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following Berkheimer and related Federal Circuit guidance, USPTO memoranda instruct examiners that such determinations require factual support. The April 19, 2018 memorandum required examiners to support findings that claim elements (or their combination) are well understood, routine, and conventional with factual determinations in the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners must support eligibility rejections with factual and reasoned explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: When issuing a §101 rejection, examiners should provide clear reasoning and (where applicable) factual support for conclusions about directedness and whether elements are routine or conventional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: US PTO memoranda and MPEP procedures emphasize training and guidance to ensure examiners faithfully apply statute and case law and to provide clarity in office actions. Public commenters urged clearer office actions and consistency among examiners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedures for identifying abstract ideas (2019 PEG and October 2019 Update)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the revised procedures in the 2019 Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidance and the October 2019 Update to identify abstract ideas and determine whether a claim is directed to a judicial exception under step 2A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 2019 PEG and October 2019 Update revised USPTO procedures for identifying abstract ideas and for determining directedness under step 2A; these updates were incorporated into MPEP chapter 2100 (sections 2103–2106) in June 2020.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity, predictability, and consistent application
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever the substantive standard for eligibility, it should be clear, predictable, and consistently applied by the USPTO and the courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a frequent theme of public comments: stakeholders across sectors requested a standard that yields uniform results and is not applied inconsistently across examiners, district courts, the PTAB, and the Federal Circuit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate §101 eligibility with other patentability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility under section 101 should not be conflated with other patentability inquiries (e.g., novelty under §102, obviousness under §103, enablement or written description under §112).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many commenters argued that the two-step framework has at times conflated §101 with other requirements and that clearer separation is desirable to avoid unpredictability and improper rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims should recite specific implementations rather than vague functional results
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims framed as specific implementations of inventive solutions are more likely to pass eligibility scrutiny than broadly claimed functional results or abstract descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supporters of the two-step framework observed that it encourages claims to be directed to specific implementations rather than vaguely claimed functional outcomes; the framework can serve as a 'forcing function' to bring greater detail and clarity to patent applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO measurement metrics for assessing impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess examination and policy impacts using measurable metrics such as allowance rate (allowances over disposals), first-office-action §101 rejection rates, and examination uncertainty (variation among examiners within a technology area).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO's 'Adjusting to Alice' report used these metrics and found a 31% increase in first-action §101 rejections in the 18 months after Alice, a 26% increase in examination uncertainty, and subsequent reductions after USPTO guidance (e.g., a 25% decrease in first-action eligibility rejections and a 44% decrease in uncertainty after the 2019 PEG).

rubrics_metrics.name: Define and measure 'exposed technologies' for sectoral exposure analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: For analyses of which industries are affected by eligibility jurisprudence, define 'exposed technologies' as patent classifications appearing in Federal Circuit and Supreme Court cases involving abstract ideas, laws of nature, or natural phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office of the Chief Economist used this definition to measure exposure and found increasing shares of patents in exposed technologies across U.S. industries; as of 2020, 46% of patents issued to U.S. companies were in exposed technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI-specific eligibility sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: AI-related inventions may be at risk of being characterized as methods of organizing human activity, mental processes, or mathematical concepts and therefore ineligible unless claims recite 'significantly more' than judicial exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public Views on AI and IP Policy reported stakeholder concerns that many AI inventions could be treated as abstract ideas under Alice; USPTO analyses (Inventing AI; allowance-rate studies) tracked differential impacts on AI-containing applications and the effect of guidance in restoring allowance rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative remedies to improve consistency and clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendations for the USPTO include increasing examiner consistency, providing clearer guidance, more examples and thorough analyses, and enhanced training for examiners on applying the two-step framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public commenters urged administrative actions (rather than or in addition to legislative changes) to reduce inconsistent application of the framework; the USPTO responded with guidance updates, roundtables, and reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-step framework as a tool against overly broad patents and abusive litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: The two-step framework can be used to challenge overly broad claims and to defend against abusive lawsuits by patent assertion entities (PAEs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some commenters viewed Alice and its subsequent application as beneficial for weeding out overly broad patents and reducing abusive litigation tactics, thereby improving the patent system's functioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate guidance into MPEP and examiner practice (procedural compliance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow USPTO memoranda, the 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance, the 2019 PEG, the October 2019 Update, and MPEP §§2103–2106 for examination procedure and training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO incorporated the revised eligibility guidance into chapter 2100 of the MPEP (incorporation completed June 2020). Examiners are directed to use these materials and related memoranda when applying eligibility standards.
